# Chores 06

Continuation of [chores-05](chores-05.md). Records landed work;
conventions in
[agent-data/notes.md](../../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions)
and [cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## Table of Contents

- [feat: dynamic warmup](#feat-dynamic-warmup)

## feat: dynamic warmup

- [[N]] 0.24.0-0 chore: open the dynamic-warmup cycle

The 0.24.0 cycle: replace the fixed `WARMUP = 10_000` step count
in `harness.rs` with warm-until-stable. A fixed count's
wall-clock scales with step cost, so the fastest benches warm
~10 us against frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of
ms and `pick_inner` sizes mid-ramp (the 7600x F diagnosis,
[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run)),
and a timing-only "did it end settled" test can issue a vacuous
A while the box dwells one P-state below the top (measured
2026-07-29 [[1]]). The design accumulated in the Todo entry over
2026-07-27 to 2026-08-01; the subsections below are its record,
plus the decisions made at pickup (2026-08-02). First cycle run
on a topic bookmark (`dynamic-warmup`).

### One warm loop, three policies

The end state, decided 2026-08-01: one parameterized warm loop.
Step the bench, probe periodically, stop when the exit condition
holds. The harness's three warms become policies over that one
mechanism:

- the per-run warmup exits when the trailing window grades A,
  or at the cap
- the process warm (`process_warm`) exits on the `--settle-time`
  budget
- the block warm (`run_blocked`'s 2 ms spin) is the same loop
  with a fixed-time exit and probing disabled

`process_warm` and `warmup_and_probe` already share one probe
series, prober and time origin; this completes the fusion
instead of adding a fourth variant.

Terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the 0.22.0-4
"loop-only passes" sense), a short, unrecorded, timed burst of
bench steps yielding one floor. Not a "probe": `TProbe` is the
measurement instrument, and the "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0
cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair frame measurement.

### The exit condition: grade the trailing window

Rather than K agreeing floors, grade a *sliding window* over
the warmup probe series and warm until the trailing window
reads A, or the cap (design 2026-07-28). The exit condition and
the warmup letter become one computation:

- exit on A means the run started post-ramp by construction
- hitting the cap reports whatever the window actually scored,
  the "run started unstable" signal, not a silent proceed
- window length takes the same "minimum count or minimum wall
  time, whichever is larger" shape as pass length: count
  because the split detector needs 4 points a side, wall time
  because the ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon
- signals: spread, drift, step; `interference` is the weak one
  [[2]]
- the minimum wall span is load-bearing: a window can be far
  shorter than what it certifies (`min-now`'s 16 warmup probes
  span ~17 us against a transition arriving at ~800 ms), so
  agreement alone certifies nothing

Floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
(in)stability; a warm box exits near-immediately.

Convergence is agreement, not direction. The 3900X is bistable
(2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid repetition
climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter), low-duty isolated
runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and transitions straddle
windows in *both* directions; a fixed warmup absorbs only
transitions shorter than itself, whatever their sign.

The hard cap sits at governor scale (a few hundred ms; exact
constant measured on both boxes during the rung). The cap
doubles as the estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard Todo
wants, so slow and non-converging benches share one diagnostic
exit.

### Sizing fusion

The warmup pass *is* the step-cost sizing pass: the converged
floor is the sizing input, so sizing is post-ramp by
construction and convergence is tested on the number actually
consumed. The `estimate_step_cost` phase folds into the warm
loop; the micro-probe supplies the frame input, run after
convergence.

Slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
(minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is larger)
so a floor is never one sample. The cap exit then distinguishes
"floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge signal) from "too slow to
certify" (proceed, label the run uncertified: at `inner = 1`
sizing can't be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes
are low there).

### Read the clock, not just the timing

Steadiness cannot tell "settled at the top" from "dwelling at
an intermediate P-state", because a dwell *is* steady. Measured
2026-07-29 on the 7600x [[1]]: the trailing window graded A
while the box held 4841 MHz for ~0.75 s, then stepped +12.4%
inside the run. This was the strongest argument for making the
clock reading part of the exit condition rather than an
optional extra, and the rung is in scope (decided 2026-08-02).

- delivered frequency is an unprivileged sysfs read on both AMD
  boxes (`cpufreq/cpuinfo_avg_freq`); the ramp is ~150-200 ms
- gate on **clock stability under load**, never on a fraction
  of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: a threshold would need tuning between
  96.1% (3900X) and 99.7% (7600x) sustained, and a
  thermally-limited laptop plateaus lower still while that
  plateau is its honest clock
- optional by construction: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is
  amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq`
  reports requested rather than delivered, so read where

wall-clock scales with step cost, so the fastest benches warm
~10 us against frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of

and a timing-only "did it end settled" test can issue a vacuous
A while the box dwells one P-state below the top (measured
2026-07-29 [[1]]). The design accumulated in the Todo entry over
2026-07-27 to 2026-08-01; the subsections below are its record,
plus the decisions made at pickup (2026-08-02). First cycle run
on a topic bookmark (`dynamic-warmup`).

### One warm loop, three policies

The end state, decided 2026-08-01: one parameterized warm loop.
Step the bench, probe periodically, stop when the exit condition
holds. The harness's three warms become policies over that one
mechanism:

- the per-run warmup exits when the trailing window grades A,
  or at the cap
- the process warm (`process_warm`) exits on the `--settle-time`
  budget
- the block warm (`run_blocked`'s 2 ms spin) is the same loop
  with a fixed-time exit and probing disabled

`process_warm` and `warmup_and_probe` already share one probe
series, prober and time origin; this completes the fusion
instead of adding a fourth variant.

Terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the 0.22.0-4
"loop-only passes" sense), a short, unrecorded, timed burst of
bench steps yielding one floor. Not a "probe": `TProbe` is the
measurement instrument, and the "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0
cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair frame measurement.

### The exit condition: grade the trailing window

Rather than K agreeing floors, grade a *sliding window* over
the warmup probe series and warm until the trailing window
reads A, or the cap (design 2026-07-28). The exit condition and
the warmup letter become one computation:

- exit on A means the run started post-ramp by construction
- hitting the cap reports whatever the window actually scored,
  the "run started unstable" signal, not a silent proceed
- window length takes the same "minimum count or minimum wall
  time, whichever is larger" shape as pass length: count
  because the split detector needs 4 points a side, wall time
  because the ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon
- signals: spread, drift, step; `interference` is the weak one
  [[2]]
- the minimum wall span is load-bearing: a window can be far
  shorter than what it certifies (`min-now`'s 16 warmup probes
  span ~17 us against a transition arriving at ~800 ms), so
  agreement alone certifies nothing

Floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
(in)stability; a warm box exits near-immediately.

Convergence is agreement, not direction. The 3900X is bistable
(2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid repetition
climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter), low-duty isolated
runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and transitions straddle
windows in *both* directions; a fixed warmup absorbs only
transitions shorter than itself, whatever their sign.

constant measured on both boxes during the rung). The cap
doubles as the estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard Todo
wants, so slow and non-converging benches share one diagnostic
exit.

The warmup pass *is* the step-cost sizing pass: the converged
floor is the sizing input, so sizing is post-ramp by
construction and convergence is tested on the number actually
consumed. The `estimate_step_cost` phase folds into the warm
loop; the micro-probe supplies the frame input, run after
convergence.

Slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
(minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is larger)
so a floor is never one sample. The cap exit then distinguishes
"floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge signal) from "too slow to
certify" (proceed, label the run uncertified: at `inner = 1`

are low there).

content.text:
Fair challenge, and the dogfood log has a test for exactly this: multi-commit is earned only when each rung is independently valuable and revertable, and "one deliverable, several files" is single-commit shaped no matter how many edits it takes.

Honest assessment of the size: the mechanism is localized — almost everything lives in `harness.rs` (the three warm sites, `pick_inner`, `estimate_step_cost`), with small satellite edits in `main.rs` (the flag deletion), a new sysfs read, and the report line. Probably 400-600 changed lines total. So you're right that it's not large. But it isn't *one* deliverable: it's one refactor plus four distinct behavior changes (exit condition, sizing input, warm placement, clock input), and in a measurement tool each behavior change can silently move numbers. If a bench reads differently after this cycle, "which of the five changes did it" is the question we'll want history to answer. That's the argument for rungs here, and it's different from the rejected four-rung ladder in the log, where every intermediate state was half-reshaped — each rung here leaves a complete working harness.

That said, my 6-rung ladder was padded. Two merges make it tighter without losing the bisection value:

- **-2 and -3 are one design, not two.** "The warmup pass is the sizing pass" isn't an add-on to the dynamic exit; it's what the loop *is*. Building the dynamic exit at -2 and rewiring sizing at -3 means reworking the same 100 lines twice.
- **-6 mostly evaporates.** Once exit-on-A lands, the warmup letter and settle line change at -2 by construction, and the `-v` probe table is a debugging aid we'll want *while* building -2, not after. The selftest-observable tweak rides with it.

Compressed ladder, four commits of substance:

- 0.24.0-0 `chore: open the dynamic-warmup cycle` (this commit)
- 0.24.0-1 `refactor: one parameterized warm loop` — behavior unchanged, tests pin it
- 0.24.0-2 `feat: warm until the trailing window grades A` — the dynamic exit *with* sizing fusion, the settle/`-v` reporting, cap-as-signal, slow-bench path
- 0.24.0-3 `feat: warm where the bench runs` — pin + `--no-pin-cal` deletion
- 0.24.0-4 `feat: read the clock during warmup`
- 0.24.0 `feat: dynamic warmup` — close-out, full validation, selftest on hardware

The minimum split I'd defend is even smaller: keep -1 (behavior-preserving refactor) separate from everything else, because "the numbers moved but the refactor was clean" versus "the refactor itself moved them" is the attribution that matters most. Collapsing further to a true single-commit cycle would work mechanically, but one commit holding a refactor plus four behavior changes to the measuring apparatus is the shape I'd regret during the first weird benchmark result.

The plain version: the code footprint is small, but it's five separable changes to the thing that produces the numbers, and keeping them as separate commits is what lets us later tell which change moved a result. I'd go with the compressed six-commit ladder above; happy to shrink it more if you weigh review overhead higher.

   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).

   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is

(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.

- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token

or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*

[After push or squash-push](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Verify bookmark tracking, the bot-published
            invariant, and sync state
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-work:     Commit the work repo
          - commit-bot:      Commit the `.claude` bot repo (skipped if empty)
          - bookmark-set:    Advance each repo's bookmark to its `@-`: work →
            `<bookmark>`, bot → `main`
          - push-work:       `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - squash-push-bot: In-process squash of `.claude`'s trailing session
            writes + push `main`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by
  the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

match matches.len() {

        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]

# Chores 06

Continuation of [chores-05](chores-05.md). Records landed work;
conventions in
[agent-data/notes.md](../../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions)
and [cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## Table of Contents

- [feat: dynamic warmup](#feat-dynamic-warmup)

## feat: dynamic warmup

- [[N]] 0.24.0-0 chore: open the dynamic-warmup cycle

The 0.24.0 cycle: replace the fixed `WARMUP = 10_000` step count
in `harness.rs` with warm-until-stable. A fixed count's
wall-clock scales with step cost, so the fastest benches warm
~10 us against frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of
ms and `pick_inner` sizes mid-ramp (the 7600x F diagnosis,
[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run)),
and a timing-only "did it end settled" test can issue a vacuous
A while the box dwells one P-state below the top (measured
2026-07-29 [[1]]). The design accumulated in the Todo entry over
2026-07-27 to 2026-08-01; the subsections below are its record,
plus the decisions made at pickup (2026-08-02). First cycle run
on a topic bookmark (`dynamic-warmup`).

### One warm loop, three policies

The end state, decided 2026-08-01: one parameterized warm loop.
Step the bench, probe periodically, stop when the exit condition
holds. The harness's three warms become policies over that one
mechanism:

- the per-run warmup exits when the trailing window grades A,
  or at the cap
- the process warm (`process_warm`) exits on the `--settle-time`
  budget
- the block warm (`run_blocked`'s 2 ms spin) is the same loop
  with a fixed-time exit and probing disabled

`process_warm` and `warmup_and_probe` already share one probe
series, prober and time origin; this completes the fusion
instead of adding a fourth variant.

Terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the 0.22.0-4
"loop-only passes" sense), a short, unrecorded, timed burst of
bench steps yielding one floor. Not a "probe": `TProbe` is the
measurement instrument, and the "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0
cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair frame measurement.

### The exit condition: grade the trailing window

Rather than K agreeing floors, grade a *sliding window* over
the warmup probe series and warm until the trailing window
reads A, or the cap (design 2026-07-28). The exit condition and
the warmup letter become one computation:

- exit on A means the run started post-ramp by construction
- hitting the cap reports whatever the window actually scored,
  the "run started unstable" signal, not a silent proceed
- window length takes the same "minimum count or minimum wall
  time, whichever is larger" shape as pass length: count
  because the split detector needs 4 points a side, wall time
  because the ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon
- signals: spread, drift, step; `interference` is the weak one
  [[2]]
- the minimum wall span is load-bearing: a window can be far
  shorter than what it certifies (`min-now`'s 16 warmup probes
  span ~17 us against a transition arriving at ~800 ms), so
  agreement alone certifies nothing

Floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
(in)stability; a warm box exits near-immediately.

Convergence is agreement, not direction. The 3900X is bistable
(2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid repetition
climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter), low-duty isolated
runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and transitions straddle
windows in *both* directions; a fixed warmup absorbs only
transitions shorter than itself, whatever their sign.

The hard cap sits at governor scale (a few hundred ms; exact
constant measured on both boxes during the rung). The cap
doubles as the estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard Todo
wants, so slow and non-converging benches share one diagnostic
exit.

### Sizing fusion

The warmup pass *is* the step-cost sizing pass: the converged
floor is the sizing input, so sizing is post-ramp by
construction and convergence is tested on the number actually
consumed. The `estimate_step_cost` phase folds into the warm
loop; the micro-probe supplies the frame input, run after
convergence.

Slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
(minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is larger)
so a floor is never one sample. The cap exit then distinguishes
"floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge signal) from "too slow to
certify" (proceed, label the run uncertified: at `inner = 1`
sizing can't be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes
are low there).

### Read the clock, not just the timing

Steadiness cannot tell "settled at the top" from "dwelling at
an intermediate P-state", because a dwell *is* steady. Measured
2026-07-29 on the 7600x [[1]]: the trailing window graded A
while the box held 4841 MHz for ~0.75 s, then stepped +12.4%
inside the run. This was the strongest argument for making the
clock reading part of the exit condition rather than an
optional extra, and the rung is in scope (decided 2026-08-02).

- delivered frequency is an unprivileged sysfs read on both AMD
  boxes (`cpufreq/cpuinfo_avg_freq`); the ramp is ~150-200 ms
- gate on **clock stability under load**, never on a fraction
  of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: a threshold would need tuning between
  96.1% (3900X) and 99.7% (7600x) sustained, and a
  thermally-limited laptop plateaus lower still while that
  plateau is its honest clock
- optional by construction: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is
  amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq`
  reports requested rather than delivered, so read where
  present and fall back to timing-only
- report the ratio, do not grade on it

`qualify-environment`'s verdict is not usable as a gate until
this cycle lands: it reads NOT QUALIFIED on any amd-pstate-epp
box that dwells then boosts, which is to say on a healthy idle
machine [[1]]. Fixing the exit condition fixes the selftest at
the same time, since its observable is this grade.

### Placement: warm where the bench runs

Decided 2026-08-02: the warm follows the bench's pin. Warm on
`pin[0]` when `--pin` is set, else wherever the scheduler has
main (a busy thread stays put, and the warm state lands on the
core that measures). The CPU0-default tick-rate warm pin and
`--no-pin-cal` are deleted rather than justified.

- CPU0 is measurably the kernel's busiest core on the 3900X
  (2026-07-29, cumulative per-CPU interrupts: 4.1M `LOC`
  against ~0.6M on CPU11/CPU23, 6.2M `CAL` against ~0.6M, 4-6x
  the `RES`, 3x the `TLB`; no `irqbalance`). CPU0 is the boot
  CPU and the `nohz_full` housekeeping CPU, so this is expected
  rather than a quirk of this box
- the pin did not matter for the tick-rate read (a ratio of TSC
  ticks to monotonic ns over ~10 ms: interruptions inflate both
  sides and cancel, ~8e-7 spread across cores), so the current
  default was harmless, not correct; it would have mattered
  here, where warmup becomes a real timing phase converging on
  per-core frequency state
- the rejected alternative, a topology-aware "not the boot CPU,
  and a full-frequency core" pin, adds machinery this cycle
  does not need; it stays with the topology Todo. "Use the last
  core" folklore was already rejected there (hybrid parts put
  E-cores at high indices)

### Report shape

Normal output carries one warmup line: letter plus **settle
time**, a real machine characteristic. `-v` shows the complete
warmup picture, the per-probe table with the ramp's shape. The
qualification selftest reading a table of settle times across
respawns is a better observable than a table of blended
letters.

### Acceptance test

`tests/qualify_environment.rs` (landed 0.23.0-1, simplified to
one loop 2026-07-28): `#[ignore]`d integration test spawning
the real binary per run (`CARGO_BIN_EXE`), one loop of 10
back-to-back runs. The loop's own load provokes the transition;
verdict: median >= B and zero runs with drift/repeat at D/F.
Reproduced failing 2026-07-27 on the 3900X (repeat F on the
climb run); `IIAC_PERF_BIN` pins a saved failing build. Part of
this cycle's close-out validation.

### Deferred: start-vs-end differential QC

Repeat the warmup pass at run end and compare floors (never
absolute, never subtracted) as a "did the box shift" check.
Deferred at pickup (2026-08-02): the run already carries seam
probes across its whole span and the run grade's drift/step
signals answer the same question; revisit if batch data shows
frame shifts need separating from per-iteration shifts. The
N-sweep slope/intercept decomposition likewise stays an idea.

# References

[1]: /notes/chores/chores-05.md#the-7600x-stopped-passing-and-the-grade-is-why
[2]: /notes/chores/chores-05.md#the-clock-behind-the-anomaly

532	/// warmup-side counterpart to [`BatchSummary`].
533	///

573	    pub over_pairs: u64,
574	}

577	/// batch seam allocates nothing.
578	struct Prober {
579	    /// Per-group mean pair cost (ps), sorted in place.
580	    groups: Vec<u64>,
581	    /// Every individual pair's own reading (ns) — the census
582	    /// population.
583	    pairs: Vec<u32>,
584	}

586	impl Prober {
587	    /// Prober with both buffers sized for one probe.
588	    fn new() -> Self {
589	        Self {
590	            groups: Vec::with_capacity(PROBE_GROUPS),
591	            pairs: Vec::with_capacity(PROBE_GROUPS * PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS),
592	        }
593	    }
594	
595	    /// Run one ~256 µs micro-probe: time [`PROBE_GROUPS`] groups
596	    /// of [`PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS`] back-to-back timer pairs (empty
597	    /// timed intervals) and summarize the per-pair distribution.
598	    ///
599	    /// - `since` anchors [`ProbeSummary::t_start_s`], so every
600	    ///   probe in a run shares one time origin.
601	    /// - The floor is a low quantile, not the minimum: it rejects
602	    ///   one-sided interference (preemption only ever inflates a
603	    ///   group) while staying off the exact edge.
604	    /// - **Two resolutions on purpose.** Floor, spread, drift and
605	    ///   step read *group* means, where the timer's 1 ns quantum
606	    ///   is ~0.06% of a ~1.6 µs group rather than ~4% of a single
607	    ///   pair. The census instead counts *individual* pairs,
608	    ///   because a group mean hides anything smaller than
609	    ///   ~800 ns — an intrusion has to survive being averaged
610	    ///   over 64 pairs to register. A census threshold sits far
611	    ///   above the 1 ns quantum, so counting pairs costs the
612	    ///   census nothing and each pair's reading is already in
613	    ///   hand.
614	    fn probe(&mut self, since: std::time::Instant) -> ProbeSummary {
615	        let t_start_s = since.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64 / 1e9;
616	        self.groups.clear();
617	        self.pairs.clear();
618	        for _ in 0..PROBE_GROUPS {
619	            let group_start = std::time::Instant::now();
620	            for _ in 0..PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS {
621	                let start = std::time::Instant::now();
622	                self.pairs.push(start.elapsed().as_nanos() as u32);
623	            }
624	            let total_ns = group_start.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64;
625	            self.groups
626	                .push((total_ns * PS_PER_NS / PROBE_GROUP_PAIRS as f64) as u64);
627	        }
628	        self.groups.sort_unstable();
629	
630	        let floor_q_ps = quantile_at(&self.groups, ENV_FLOOR_Q).max(1);
631	        let spread_q_ps = quantile_at(&self.groups, ENV_SPREAD_Q);
632	        let sum: u128 = self.groups.iter().map(|&g| u128::from(g)).sum();
633	        let mean_ps = sum as f64 / self.groups.len() as f64;
634	
635	        let cut_ps = over_floor_cut(floor_q_ps, ENV_OVER_ADD_PS);
636	        let cut_ns = cut_ps as f64 / PS_PER_NS;
637	        let over_pairs = self
638	            .pairs
639	            .iter()
640	            .filter(|&&p| f64::from(p) > cut_ns)
641	            .count() as u64;
642	
643	        ProbeSummary {
644	            t_start_s,
645	            groups: self.groups.len() as u64,
646	            floor_q_ps,
647	            spread_q_ps,
648	            mean_ps,
649	            pairs: self.pairs.len() as u64,
650	            over_pairs,
651	        }
652	    }
653	}

# Chores 06

Continuation of [chores-05](chores-05.md). Records landed work;
conventions in
[agent-data/notes.md](../../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions)
and [cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

## Table of Contents

- [feat: dynamic warmup](#feat-dynamic-warmup)

## feat: dynamic warmup

- [[N]] 0.24.0-0 chore: open the dynamic-warmup cycle
- [[N]] 0.24.0-1 refactor: one parameterized warm loop

The 0.24.0 cycle: replace the fixed `WARMUP = 10_000` step count
in `harness.rs` with warm-until-stable. A fixed count's
wall-clock scales with step cost, so the fastest benches warm
~10 us against frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of
ms and `pick_inner` sizes mid-ramp (the 7600x F diagnosis,
[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run)),
and a timing-only "did it end settled" test can issue a vacuous
A while the box dwells one P-state below the top (measured
2026-07-29 [[1]]). The design accumulated in the Todo entry over
2026-07-27 to 2026-08-01; the subsections below are its record,
plus the decisions made at pickup (2026-08-02). First cycle run
on a topic bookmark (`dynamic-warmup`).

### One warm loop, three policies

The end state, decided 2026-08-01: one parameterized warm loop.
Step the bench, probe periodically, stop when the exit condition
holds. The harness's three warms become policies over that one
mechanism:

- the per-run warmup exits when the trailing window grades A,
  or at the cap
- the process warm (`process_warm`) exits on the `--settle-time`
  budget
- the block warm (`run_blocked`'s 2 ms spin) is the same loop
  with a fixed-time exit and probing disabled

`process_warm` and `warmup_and_probe` already share one probe
series, prober and time origin; this completes the fusion
instead of adding a fourth variant.

Terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the 0.22.0-4
"loop-only passes" sense), a short, unrecorded, timed burst of
bench steps yielding one floor. Not a "probe": `TProbe` is the
measurement instrument, and the "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0
cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair frame measurement.

### The exit condition: grade the trailing window

Rather than K agreeing floors, grade a *sliding window* over
the warmup probe series and warm until the trailing window
reads A, or the cap (design 2026-07-28). The exit condition and
the warmup letter become one computation:

- exit on A means the run started post-ramp by construction
- hitting the cap reports whatever the window actually scored,
  the "run started unstable" signal, not a silent proceed
- window length takes the same "minimum count or minimum wall
  time, whichever is larger" shape as pass length: count
  because the split detector needs 4 points a side, wall time
  because the ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon
- signals: spread, drift, step; `interference` is the weak one
  [[2]]
- the minimum wall span is load-bearing: a window can be far
  shorter than what it certifies (`min-now`'s 16 warmup probes
  span ~17 us against a transition arriving at ~800 ms), so
  agreement alone certifies nothing

Floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
(in)stability; a warm box exits near-immediately.

Convergence is agreement, not direction. The 3900X is bistable
(2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid repetition
climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter), low-duty isolated
runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and transitions straddle
windows in *both* directions; a fixed warmup absorbs only
transitions shorter than itself, whatever their sign.

The hard cap sits at governor scale (a few hundred ms; exact
constant measured on both boxes during the rung). The cap
doubles as the estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard Todo
wants, so slow and non-converging benches share one diagnostic
exit.

### Sizing fusion

The warmup pass *is* the step-cost sizing pass: the converged
floor is the sizing input, so sizing is post-ramp by
construction and convergence is tested on the number actually
consumed. The `estimate_step_cost` phase folds into the warm
loop; the micro-probe supplies the frame input, run after
convergence.

Slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
(minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is larger)
so a floor is never one sample. The cap exit then distinguishes
"floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge signal) from "too slow to
certify" (proceed, label the run uncertified: at `inner = 1`
sizing can't be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes
are low there).

### Read the clock, not just the timing

Steadiness cannot tell "settled at the top" from "dwelling at
an intermediate P-state", because a dwell *is* steady. Measured
2026-07-29 on the 7600x [[1]]: the trailing window graded A
while the box held 4841 MHz for ~0.75 s, then stepped +12.4%
inside the run. This was the strongest argument for making the
clock reading part of the exit condition rather than an
optional extra, and the rung is in scope (decided 2026-08-02).

- delivered frequency is an unprivileged sysfs read on both AMD
  boxes (`cpufreq/cpuinfo_avg_freq`); the ramp is ~150-200 ms
- gate on **clock stability under load**, never on a fraction
  of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: a threshold would need tuning between
  96.1% (3900X) and 99.7% (7600x) sustained, and a
  thermally-limited laptop plateaus lower still while that
  plateau is its honest clock
- optional by construction: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is
  amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq`
  reports requested rather than delivered, so read where
  present and fall back to timing-only
- report the ratio, do not grade on it

`qualify-environment`'s verdict is not usable as a gate until
this cycle lands: it reads NOT QUALIFIED on any amd-pstate-epp
box that dwells then boosts, which is to say on a healthy idle
machine [[1]]. Fixing the exit condition fixes the selftest at
the same time, since its observable is this grade.

### Placement: warm where the bench runs

Decided 2026-08-02: the warm follows the bench's pin. Warm on
`pin[0]` when `--pin` is set, else wherever the scheduler has
main (a busy thread stays put, and the warm state lands on the
core that measures). The CPU0-default tick-rate warm pin and
`--no-pin-cal` are deleted rather than justified.

- CPU0 is measurably the kernel's busiest core on the 3900X
  (2026-07-29, cumulative per-CPU interrupts: 4.1M `LOC`
  against ~0.6M on CPU11/CPU23, 6.2M `CAL` against ~0.6M, 4-6x
  the `RES`, 3x the `TLB`; no `irqbalance`). CPU0 is the boot
  CPU and the `nohz_full` housekeeping CPU, so this is expected
  rather than a quirk of this box
- the pin did not matter for the tick-rate read (a ratio of TSC
  ticks to monotonic ns over ~10 ms: interruptions inflate both
  sides and cancel, ~8e-7 spread across cores), so the current
  default was harmless, not correct; it would have mattered
  here, where warmup becomes a real timing phase converging on
  per-core frequency state
- the rejected alternative, a topology-aware "not the boot CPU,
  and a full-frequency core" pin, adds machinery this cycle
  does not need; it stays with the topology Todo. "Use the last
  core" folklore was already rejected there (hybrid parts put
  E-cores at high indices)

### Report shape

Normal output carries one warmup line: letter plus **settle
time**, a real machine characteristic. `-v` shows the complete
warmup picture, the per-probe table with the ramp's shape. The
qualification selftest reading a table of settle times across
respawns is a better observable than a table of blended
letters.

### Acceptance test

`tests/qualify_environment.rs` (landed 0.23.0-1, simplified to
one loop 2026-07-28): `#[ignore]`d integration test spawning
the real binary per run (`CARGO_BIN_EXE`), one loop of 10
back-to-back runs. The loop's own load provokes the transition;
verdict: median >= B and zero runs with drift/repeat at D/F.
Reproduced failing 2026-07-27 on the 3900X (repeat F on the
climb run); `IIAC_PERF_BIN` pins a saved failing build. Part of
this cycle's close-out validation.

### Deferred: start-vs-end differential QC

Repeat the warmup pass at run end and compare floors (never
absolute, never subtracted) as a "did the box shift" check.
Deferred at pickup (2026-08-02): the run already carries seam
probes across its whole span and the run grade's drift/step
signals answer the same question; revisit if batch data shows
frame shifts need separating from per-iteration shifts. The
N-sweep slope/intercept decomposition likewise stays an idea.

# References

[1]: /notes/chores/chores-05.md#the-7600x-stopped-passing-and-the-grade-is-why
[2]: /notes/chores/chores-05.md#the-clock-behind-the-anomaly

  (2026-07-29, cumulative per-CPU interrupts: 4.1M `LOC`
  against ~0.6M on CPU11/CPU23, 6.2M `CAL` against ~0.6M, 4-6x
  the `RES`, 3x the `TLB`; no `irqbalance`). CPU0 is the boot
  CPU and the `nohz_full` housekeeping CPU, so this is expected
  rather than a quirk of this box
- the pin did not matter for the tick-rate read (a ratio of TSC
  ticks to monotonic ns over ~10 ms: interruptions inflate both
  sides and cancel, ~8e-7 spread across cores), so the current
  default was harmless, not correct; it would have mattered
  here, where warmup becomes a real timing phase converging on
  per-core frequency state
- the rejected alternative, a topology-aware "not the boot CPU,
  and a full-frequency core" pin, adds machinery this cycle
  does not need; it stays with the topology Todo. "Use the last
  core" folklore was already rejected there (hybrid parts put
  E-cores at high indices)

### Report shape

Normal output carries one warmup line: letter plus **settle
time**, a real machine characteristic. `-v` shows the complete
warmup picture, the per-probe table with the ramp's shape. The
qualification selftest reading a table of settle times across
respawns is a better observable than a table of blended
letters.

### Acceptance test

`tests/qualify_environment.rs` (landed 0.23.0-1, simplified to
one loop 2026-07-28): `#[ignore]`d integration test spawning
the real binary per run (`CARGO_BIN_EXE`), one loop of 10
back-to-back runs. The loop's own load provokes the transition;
verdict: median >= B and zero runs with drift/repeat at D/F.
Reproduced failing 2026-07-27 on the 3900X (repeat F on the
climb run); `IIAC_PERF_BIN` pins a saved failing build. Part of
this cycle's close-out validation.

### Deferred: start-vs-end differential QC

Repeat the warmup pass at run end and compare floors (never
absolute, never subtracted) as a "did the box shift" check.
Deferred at pickup (2026-08-02): the run already carries seam
probes across its whole span and the run grade's drift/step
signals answer the same question; revisit if batch data shows
frame shifts need separating from per-iteration shifts. The
N-sweep slope/intercept decomposition likewise stays an idea.

`qualify-environment`'s verdict is not usable as a gate until
this cycle lands: it reads NOT QUALIFIED on any amd-pstate-epp
box that dwells then boosts, which is to say on a healthy idle
machine [[1]]. Fixing the exit condition fixes the selftest at
the same time, since its observable is this grade.

As built at -4: `src/freq.rs` reads `cpuinfo_avg_freq` on the
calling thread's current CPU (`sched_getcpu`), one sample per
warmup probe, kept parallel to the probe series across the
process-warm handoff.

- the exit gains a second gate: timing-A *and* clock held
  within 1% (`FREQ_STABLE_TOL`) across the exit window; a
  timing-steady window with a moving clock classifies Unstable
  (the dwell case, unit-tested against the 7600x numbers)
- anything short of clean same-CPU readings falls back to
  timing-only: file absent, read failure, or an unpinned main
  migrating mid-window (samples carry their CPU id)
- the ratio prints on the `-v` warmup summary line
  (`clock 4093/4674 MHz (87.6%)` measured on the 3900X, whose
  honest sustained clock is ~87% of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: live
  confirmation that a fraction-of-max threshold would misfire
  and stability-under-load is the right gate)
- review point: the ratio is `-v`-only for now; the design
  said "report it", and the normal grade block's columns are
  parsed positionally by qualify, so adding it there was
  deferred to review

content.text:
All four rungs are done and committed locally on top of the pushed prep commit — nothing was pushed. Here's the review picture for when you're back.

**The chain** (`jj log -r 'main..@'`; scratch titles, no ochids — publishing happens rung-by-rung with `vc-x1 push` after your review):

- **-1 `refactor: one parameterized warm loop`** — `WarmPass` / `WarmSeries` / `warm_loop`; the three warms became policies with their old exits; behavior-identical, pinned by the full suite before anything moved.
- **-2 `feat: warm until the trailing window grades A`** — the dynamic exit plus sizing fusion (`estimate_step_cost` deleted; sizing reads the exit window's best pass), the `-v` per-probe table, and the cap/uncertified paths. The graded tail and the exit window are now literally the same slice.
- **-3 `feat: warm where the bench runs`** — `--no-pin-cal`, the CPU0 warm pin, and pin.rs's save/restore pair deleted; main pins to `pin[0]` only when `--pin` is given; the Setup cell renamed `warm pin` -> `main pin`; README's five mentions reworked.
- **-4 `feat: read the clock during warmup`** — new `src/freq.rs` (`cpuinfo_avg_freq` only, deliberately no `scaling_cur_freq` fallback); clock stability across the exit window joins the exit condition; migration or absent file falls back to timing-only; ratio prints on the `-v` line.

**Provisional constants to review** (all doc-commented in harness.rs): pass minimums 8 steps / 1 ms, window minimums 8 probes / 50 ms, cap 400 ms, clock tolerance 1%. The biggest judgment call: the exit window **replaces** the fixed 300 ms `WARMUP_TAIL_SECONDS`, so a settled warm now costs ~51 ms per run instead of ~4 ms fixed.

**Flagged observations**: two benches in an `all` sweep printed grade A beside "not settled" (a within-window wobble the grade's thresholds accept but the 1% settle band doesn't — worth deciding whether the two should align); the clock ratio is `-v`-only for now since the grade block's columns are positionally parsed by qualify.

**The acceptance run** (chores-06 has the full note, sitting uncommitted in `@` as close-out material): warmup column now reads 9 A + 1 B with honest settle times — the vacuous-A defect is gone. The verdict is still NOT QUALIFIED on the 3900X, but for a truthful run-side reason: bistable transitions landing mid-run on 3 of 10 runs. That raises two close-out questions — whether the verdict's transition rule fits a box with this trait, and whether the 400 ms cap should sit above the 3900X's ~1 s relaxation re-ramp. The 7600x (where the dwell was measured) still needs its pass; that's the box this cycle's fix is really for.

Remaining: your review of the chain, then rung-by-rung publish, then the -5 report rung is already absorbed (settle line + `-v` table landed with -2, per the compressed ladder) — so what's left is close-out: chores finalization, Done entry, full validation, and the landing-onto-main discussion.

content.text:
That's the 3900X's bistability landing mid-run, and it's the failure mode this cycle deliberately does not own — with one interesting follow-up it suggests.

Reading the two runs:

- **The warmup certificate is honest.** Both runs started settled: timing window A, clock stable, settle 0.01 s (the process warm had already carried the box to a held state). Nothing the warmup said was wrong.
- **The step arrives at seconds scale.** Unpinned it landed at ~4.0 s, pinned at ~2.1 s, both ~10% — the documented two-state flip (~9% apart, the climb under sustained rapid repetition). The env-bench and run rows agree on the time and size, so the gauge is attributing it correctly: the box moved, not the workload.
- **No warmup can absorb this one.** The trailing-window exit certifies "you start settled"; this transition needs *seconds of sustained load* to trigger — longer than the 1.5 s process warm plus the whole warm stretch — and the notes record it flipping in both directions (climb under load, sag after). A warmup long enough to provoke it reliably doesn't exist, because holding the fast state depends on the run's own duty cycle. This is exactly why the run grade kept its own drift/step signals instead of trusting the warmup letter.

So "warmup A, run F" is the system working: the F is a true statement about a machine trait, the same one that made 3 of 10 acceptance runs transition-degraded this morning. Practical mitigations on this box are the existing ones: `--blocks` (re-rolls state and shows the two levels as block means), longer `-d` so the trimmed row straddles both states, or A/B comparisons that keep duty cycle matched.

The follow-up this data argues for: **sample the clock at batch seams too**, not just during warmup. If `cpuinfo_avg_freq` visibly moves at ~2.1 s on the pinned run, the run grade's step could carry a "clock moved" attribution the way warmup now distinguishes dwell from top — turning "step 10.89% F" into "step 10.89% F (clock +9%)", which tells you at a glance it's DVFS, not interference. That's a natural small Todo (the seam probe and the freq reader both already exist); it pairs with the placement-tracking design's attribution idea. Want me to add it to TODO.md as close-out material, or leave it for your review of the cycle?

The plain version: the warmup fix is doing its job — both runs genuinely started in a steady state. What graded F is the machine changing speed partway through a five-second run, a known personality of this chip that no amount of warming up beforehand can prevent, only report honestly — which it did, down to the timestamp. The natural next step is to also watch the CPU clock during the run itself, so those mid-run speed changes get labeled as such.

That's the cycle's target case closing, and the settle number tells the whole story: **0.77 s** — the warm loop sat through the 4841 MHz dwell, caught the boost at ~0.8 s (the exact transition measured on 2026-07-29), and only then let measurement start. Before this cycle, that same box printed a vacuous warmup A while the +12% step landed *inside* the run at ~0.8 s and flunked it. Now the whole board reads A, drift and step at 0.00%, and the trimmed stdev is 0.1 ns — the box was measured entirely in its top state.

It also validates the two-gate design nicely: a timing-only window could have exited settled inside the dwell (a dwell is steady); holding until 0.77 s is the clock gate and the 50 ms span doing their jobs together.

One more data point would make the close-out case complete: the cross-respawn verdict on that box, which needs no source tree — `./iiac-perf-0.24.0-4a qualify-environment` on the 7600x. That's the observable the notes said was "not usable as a gate until this lands"; if it now reads QUALIFIED across its 10 respawns, the acceptance story is measured on both boxes (with the 3900X's remaining NOT QUALIFIED attributed to its mid-run bistability, a separate question the chores note already raises for review).

content.text:
Two things done below: the docs gap becomes a top Todo, and the blocks pair gets read and recorded — it's genuinely the best demonstration yet of what the numbers mean.

**Reading your blocks comparison** (this is exactly the interpretation the docs need to teach):

- **`--blocks 1000` (all A, CI95 0.0 ns)**: each block measures ~5 ms then sleeps 1-10 ms. That low-duty cadence never provokes the climb, so the box held its slow state (24.0 ns) for the whole 13 s — and the harness measured *that state* essentially perfectly: trimmed stdev 0.1 ns, block means agreeing to 0.0 ns. Grade A here means "internally consistent", not "the canonical number".
- **`--blocks 100` (F, step at ~5.5 s)**: 50 ms bursts are sustained enough that the box climbed into the fast state early (the band table centers on 21.4-21.8 ns), then flipped back near the end — a run straddling both states, and the grade says so.
- **Plain `-d 5` from earlier**: same story with the flip at ~2-4 s.

So the three runs aren't "one good, two bad" — they're the machine's two states (24.0 vs ~21.8, the ~9-10% bistability) being *selected by the run's own duty cycle*, with the grade honestly reporting whether the run stayed in one state or straddled. The practical rule your data demonstrates: for A/B comparisons, matched duty cycle matters more than chasing grade A, and the state difference itself is a machine characteristic worth knowing. Also worth savoring: `--blocks 1000` reading CI95 0.0 ns on an unpinned desktop is the harness working extremely well.

Adding the docs Todo at rank #1 and banking the observation in chores-06:

# custom.md - iiac-perf's project layer

The one agent-editable instruction file (see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#custommd-the-project-layer)).
Loaded after AGENTS.md; on conflict, this file wins.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
`iiac-perf`); versioning specifics in [versioning.md](notes/versioning.md).

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 4; skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`
- **Pipelines hide failures**
  - never pipe a validating command into `tail`/`grep`
  - never `&&` after a piped stage: a pipeline's status is the last command's
  - `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`: the escape hatch when a pipe is genuinely wanted

## Project conventions and overrides

- **Version advancement is scope-based: minor for architecture, patch for everything else**
  (adopted 2026-08-01, replacing the 2026-07-29 functional-vs-docs rule)
  - the test: did the *shape* of the system change, or just its contents? Minor when the
    harness's structure changes: how it measures, grades, or is organized (a subsystem added
    or removed, the pipeline reshaped, the report contract redesigned). Patch for work within
    the existing shape: new benches, incremental features, presentation, docs, notes
  - versioning.md specifies only the suffix scheme; this is the project's `X.Y.Z` advancement
    choice. The version is not a compatibility contract (binary crate, no dependents); revisit
    with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out
  - first application: the 2026-08-01 renumber (below)

- **Installed vc-x1 predates the `code` -> `work` scope rename** (checked 2026-07-31)
  - overrides the scope note in [AGENTS.md Terminology](AGENTS.md#the-dual-repo-model): use
    `--scope=code|bot|code,bot` with the installed binary
  - retire this entry when vc-x1 is upgraded past the rename
- **Acquaint routine addition: check the mailbox** (adopted 2026-07-31)
  - on acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/iiac-perf.md`; an absent file means no mail
  - the message protocol is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md`
- **Non-top-commit ochid exception dropped pending verification** (2026-07-31)
  - the pre-restructure AGENTS.md permitted `jj commit` plus a hand-written `ochid:` for a
    commit pushed later as a non-top commit, on the ground that push stamps only the topmost
    commit
  - hard rule 5 (never hand-write ochids) governs until `vc-x1 push`'s actual stamping
    behavior on multi-commit pushes is verified; if push stamps every commit it creates, the
    exception stays dead, otherwise raise it as a template finding

## Dogfood log

Dated entries on where these instructions chafed, failed, or got amended; the evidence base
for the promotion decision in the template repository (vc-x1-template).

- 2026-08-01: published history renumbered under the new scope-based advancement rule
  - mapping: 0.24.0 -> 0.23.2 (grade-block compaction: presentation within the existing
    shape), 0.24.1 -> 0.23.3 (report docs), and the punctuation sweep lands as 0.23.4;
    0.24.0 stays reserved for the next architectural change
  - executed as a jj history rewrite of the two published commits (version-of-record and
    description; ochid trailers hand-copied per the re-describe rule) plus a force-push;
    safe because this repo has a single user and no external clones
  - permanent residue: bot-repo session transcripts and reports pasted in conversation carry
    the old `iiac-perf 0.24.0` / `0.24.1` banners; this mapping is the decoder
  - process finding: the rewrite would have been free had the cycles run on a topic bookmark
    landed onto `main` after review; "always work on a branch" added to TODO.md
- 2026-08-01: `vc-x1 push --body` rejects a body whose first character is `-`
  - a file-by-file body opening with its first bullet failed twice: once at vc-x1's own clap
    (worked around with `--body=`), then again inside push's `jj commit -m <body>` (same clap
    leading-hyphen rejection), which rolled both repos back cleanly
  - workaround that also satisfies prose form: open the body with its intro line, never a
    bare bullet
  - template finding: vc-x1 should pass bodies to jj as `-m=<body>` or via stdin/file

- 2026-07-31: adopted mid-dogfood-window
  - adoption base: the template's `AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730-snapshot/` (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md,
    agent-data/), created the same day from vc-x1's live copy, the window's authority
  - local copies verified byte-identical to the snapshot at adoption (`diff -r`)
- 2026-07-31: adoption base amended before first commit
  - the snapshot's AGENTS.md gained rule 0 (read custom.md before acting) and hard-rules-first
    ordering; authored snapshot-side while vc-x1's session was live, with the pending sync to
    vc-x1 tracked in the template's snapshots.md
  - local AGENTS.md re-copied from the snapshot; pin set re-verified byte-identical
- 2026-07-31: template restructured into vc-x1-template; pin lines made generic
  - the template + coordination point is now the vc-x1-template repo: init payload in `work/`
    and `work.claude/`, discussion artifacts in `agents-protocol/`, mailboxes in `messages/`;
    the old vc-x1-work-repo-template and vc-x1-bot-repo-template are untouched pending wink's
    discussion with vc-x1
  - every "pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template" line in the pin set became "the template
    repository" (snapshot-side amendment, same pending-sync flow as rule 0)
  - local pin set re-copied; snapshot, `work/`, and this repo verified three-way byte-identical
- 2026-07-31: first push under the new rules; two checklist gaps found (the 0.23.1 push)
  - given "desc and push", the agent jumped straight to the description: cycle.md's per-commit
    checklist has no step for backfilling the previous push's chores refs, bumping the
    version-of-record, or appending the chores record, so following it verbatim skips all
    three. Proposed template fix: add them as explicit steps before "write the description"
  - rule adopted (wink): **every commit belongs to a cycle, single- or multi-commit; there is
    no out-of-cycle push.** Mid-ladder the cycle is implied; otherwise ask "single- or
    multi-step cycle?" before preparing the commit. A single-commit cycle is a bare `X.Y.Z`
    close-out, so its validation is mandatory, and with no planning phase it skips
    `## In Progress` and goes straight to chores + Done
  - convention adopted (wink): chores commit references use the **as-built ladder form** for
    every cycle (rung `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`), replacing the `Commits:` line; codified in
    agent-data/notes.md + cycle.md (snapshot-side, pending vc-x1 sync) and both
    cycle-protocol.md copies (this repo's and the template payload's); pre-existing
    `Commits:` lines are grandfathered
  - convention adopted (wink): chores files carry a **title-only `## Table of Contents`**, one
    `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording section; no versions or refs, so it
    never needs backfill (the TOC navigates, the ladder records); codified beside the ladder
    form, first instance in chores-05.md
- 2026-07-31: Todo #1 run as a single-commit cycle after a four-rung ladder was rejected
  - the proposed rungs split along implementation lines (print+parser / precision / README)
    and failed the test that makes a ladder worth having: no rung was independently valuable
    or revertable, and every intermediate state was a half-reshaped published report
  - refines the single-vs-multi question: multi-commit wants rungs that each stand alone;
    "one deliverable, several files" is single-commit shaped no matter how many edits it takes
- 2026-07-31: post-facto trapezoid experiment (0.23.0)
  - a published linear cycle was reshaped in place into the merge non-ff form with one
    `jj rebase -s` (close-out becomes the merge, rungs become the side leg, descendants
    follow); chids and ochid trailers survived, the bot repo needed nothing, and the one
    casualty was the close-out's recorded SHA, re-recorded per the backfill timing rule
  - details in chores-05.md "Post-facto trapezoid rewrite (2026-07-31)"; family-relevant if
    other repos want to adopt the trapezoid shape retroactively
  - the pre-restructure AGENTS.md is replaced (preserved in jj history, and verbatim as the
    template's AGENTS-iiac-perf.md)
  - the parked `punctuation-sweep` branch (TODO.md Todo #2) edited the old AGENTS.md; its
    AGENTS.md hunks are obsolete now that the typeable-punctuation rule ships as hard rule 8
    and prose.md, so the branch needs re-scoping to its README / TODO.md /
    notes/cycle-protocol.md conversions before landing
  - remaining pre-restructure local deltas (e.g. clap `verbatim_doc_comment` guidance) still
    need distilling into this file or proposing into the template; review findings recorded
    in the template's AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730-review-iiac-perf-f5-20260731.md

1	# Chores 06
2	
3	Continuation of [chores-05](chores-05.md). Records landed work;
4	conventions in
5	[agent-data/notes.md](../../agent-data/notes.md#chores-conventions)
6	and [cycle-protocol.md](../cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
7	
8	## Table of Contents
9	
10	- [feat: dynamic warmup](#feat-dynamic-warmup)
11	
12	## feat: dynamic warmup
13	
14	- [[N]] 0.24.0-0 chore: open the dynamic-warmup cycle
15	- [[N]] 0.24.0-1 refactor: one parameterized warm loop
16	- [[N]] 0.24.0-2 feat: warm until the trailing window grades A
17	- [[N]] 0.24.0-3 feat: warm where the bench runs
18	- [[N]] 0.24.0-4 feat: read the clock during warmup
19	
20	The 0.24.0 cycle: replace the fixed `WARMUP = 10_000` step count
21	in `harness.rs` with warm-until-stable. A fixed count's
22	wall-clock scales with step cost, so the fastest benches warm
23	~10 us against frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of
24	ms and `pick_inner` sizes mid-ramp (the 7600x F diagnosis,
25	[Replanning II](chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run)),
26	and a timing-only "did it end settled" test can issue a vacuous
27	A while the box dwells one P-state below the top (measured
28	2026-07-29 [[1]]). The design accumulated in the Todo entry over
29	2026-07-27 to 2026-08-01; the subsections below are its record,
30	plus the decisions made at pickup (2026-08-02). First cycle run
31	on a topic bookmark (`dynamic-warmup`).
32	
33	### One warm loop, three policies
34	
35	The end state, decided 2026-08-01: one parameterized warm loop.
36	Step the bench, probe periodically, stop when the exit condition
37	holds. The harness's three warms become policies over that one
38	mechanism:
39	
40	- the per-run warmup exits when the trailing window grades A,
41	  or at the cap
42	- the process warm (`process_warm`) exits on the `--settle-time`
43	  budget
44	- the block warm (`run_blocked`'s 2 ms spin) is the same loop
45	  with a fixed-time exit and probing disabled
46	
47	`process_warm` and `warmup_and_probe` already share one probe
48	series, prober and time origin; this completes the fusion
49	instead of adding a fourth variant.
50	
51	Terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the 0.22.0-4
52	"loop-only passes" sense), a short, unrecorded, timed burst of
53	bench steps yielding one floor. Not a "probe": `TProbe` is the
54	measurement instrument, and the "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0
55	cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair frame measurement.
56	
57	### The exit condition: grade the trailing window
58	
59	Rather than K agreeing floors, grade a *sliding window* over
60	the warmup probe series and warm until the trailing window
61	reads A, or the cap (design 2026-07-28). The exit condition and
62	the warmup letter become one computation:
63	
64	- exit on A means the run started post-ramp by construction
65	- hitting the cap reports whatever the window actually scored,
66	  the "run started unstable" signal, not a silent proceed
67	- window length takes the same "minimum count or minimum wall
68	  time, whichever is larger" shape as pass length: count
69	  because the split detector needs 4 points a side, wall time
70	  because the ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon
71	- signals: spread, drift, step; `interference` is the weak one
72	  [[2]]
73	- the minimum wall span is load-bearing: a window can be far
74	  shorter than what it certifies (`min-now`'s 16 warmup probes
75	  span ~17 us against a transition arriving at ~800 ms), so
76	  agreement alone certifies nothing
77	
78	Floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
79	(in)stability; a warm box exits near-immediately.
80	
81	Convergence is agreement, not direction. The 3900X is bistable
82	(2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid repetition
83	climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter), low-duty isolated
84	runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and transitions straddle
85	windows in *both* directions; a fixed warmup absorbs only
86	transitions shorter than itself, whatever their sign.
87	
88	The hard cap sits at governor scale (a few hundred ms; exact
89	constant measured on both boxes during the rung). The cap
90	doubles as the estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard Todo
91	wants, so slow and non-converging benches share one diagnostic
92	exit.
93	
94	### Sizing fusion
95	
96	The warmup pass *is* the step-cost sizing pass: the converged
97	floor is the sizing input, so sizing is post-ramp by
98	construction and convergence is tested on the number actually
99	consumed. The `estimate_step_cost` phase folds into the warm
100	loop; the micro-probe supplies the frame input, run after
101	convergence.
102	
103	Slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
104	(minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is larger)
105	so a floor is never one sample. The cap exit then distinguishes
106	"floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge signal) from "too slow to
107	certify" (proceed, label the run uncertified: at `inner = 1`
108	sizing can't be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes
109	are low there).
110	
111	### Read the clock, not just the timing
112	
113	Steadiness cannot tell "settled at the top" from "dwelling at
114	an intermediate P-state", because a dwell *is* steady. Measured
115	2026-07-29 on the 7600x [[1]]: the trailing window graded A
116	while the box held 4841 MHz for ~0.75 s, then stepped +12.4%
117	inside the run. This was the strongest argument for making the
118	clock reading part of the exit condition rather than an
119	optional extra, and the rung is in scope (decided 2026-08-02).
120	
121	- delivered frequency is an unprivileged sysfs read on both AMD
122	  boxes (`cpufreq/cpuinfo_avg_freq`); the ramp is ~150-200 ms
123	- gate on **clock stability under load**, never on a fraction
124	  of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: a threshold would need tuning between
125	  96.1% (3900X) and 99.7% (7600x) sustained, and a
126	  thermally-limited laptop plateaus lower still while that
127	  plateau is its honest clock
128	- optional by construction: `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is
129	  amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq`
130	  reports requested rather than delivered, so read where
131	  present and fall back to timing-only
132	- report the ratio, do not grade on it
133	
134	`qualify-environment`'s verdict is not usable as a gate until
135	this cycle lands: it reads NOT QUALIFIED on any amd-pstate-epp
136	box that dwells then boosts, which is to say on a healthy idle
137	machine [[1]]. Fixing the exit condition fixes the selftest at
138	the same time, since its observable is this grade.
139	
140	As built at -4: `src/freq.rs` reads `cpuinfo_avg_freq` on the
141	calling thread's current CPU (`sched_getcpu`), one sample per
142	warmup probe, kept parallel to the probe series across the
143	process-warm handoff.
144	
145	- the exit gains a second gate: timing-A *and* clock held
146	  within 1% (`FREQ_STABLE_TOL`) across the exit window; a
147	  timing-steady window with a moving clock classifies Unstable
148	  (the dwell case, unit-tested against the 7600x numbers)
149	- anything short of clean same-CPU readings falls back to
150	  timing-only: file absent, read failure, or an unpinned main
151	  migrating mid-window (samples carry their CPU id)
152	- the ratio prints on the `-v` warmup summary line
153	  (`clock 4093/4674 MHz (87.6%)` measured on the 3900X, whose
154	  honest sustained clock is ~87% of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: live
155	  confirmation that a fraction-of-max threshold would misfire
156	  and stability-under-load is the right gate)
157	- review point: the ratio is `-v`-only for now; the design
158	  said "report it", and the normal grade block's columns are
159	  parsed positionally by qualify, so adding it there was
160	  deferred to review
161	
162	### Placement: warm where the bench runs
163	
164	Decided 2026-08-02: the warm follows the bench's pin. Warm on
165	`pin[0]` when `--pin` is set, else wherever the scheduler has
166	main (a busy thread stays put, and the warm state lands on the
167	core that measures). The CPU0-default tick-rate warm pin and
168	`--no-pin-cal` are deleted rather than justified.
169	
170	- CPU0 is measurably the kernel's busiest core on the 3900X
171	  (2026-07-29, cumulative per-CPU interrupts: 4.1M `LOC`
172	  against ~0.6M on CPU11/CPU23, 6.2M `CAL` against ~0.6M, 4-6x
173	  the `RES`, 3x the `TLB`; no `irqbalance`). CPU0 is the boot
174	  CPU and the `nohz_full` housekeeping CPU, so this is expected
175	  rather than a quirk of this box
176	- the pin did not matter for the tick-rate read (a ratio of TSC
177	  ticks to monotonic ns over ~10 ms: interruptions inflate both
178	  sides and cancel, ~8e-7 spread across cores), so the current
179	  default was harmless, not correct; it would have mattered
180	  here, where warmup becomes a real timing phase converging on
181	  per-core frequency state
182	- the rejected alternative, a topology-aware "not the boot CPU,
183	  and a full-frequency core" pin, adds machinery this cycle
184	  does not need; it stays with the topology Todo. "Use the last
185	  core" folklore was already rejected there (hybrid parts put
186	  E-cores at high indices)
187	- as built at -3: main pins to `pin[0]` (and stays; it is
188	  thread 0 of every bench) only when `--pin` is given;
189	  `--no-pin-cal` and `pin.rs`'s save/restore pair are deleted;
190	  the Setup cell is renamed `warm pin` -> `main pin`, naming
191	  main's placement for warm and run both
192	
193	### Report shape
194	
195	Normal output carries one warmup line: letter plus **settle
196	time**, a real machine characteristic. `-v` shows the complete
197	warmup picture, the per-probe table with the ramp's shape. The
198	qualification selftest reading a table of settle times across
199	respawns is a better observable than a table of blended
200	letters.
201	
202	### Acceptance test
203	
204	`tests/qualify_environment.rs` (landed 0.23.0-1, simplified to
205	one loop 2026-07-28): `#[ignore]`d integration test spawning
